prompt: Which of these is a force, in the sense this lesson uses?

choices.text: This code would be cleaner with a factory
choices.why: That names a pattern and a feeling; nothing in it can be checked against the code or its history.

choices.text: Each new member category means editing the fine function
choices.why: Right. Something changes and the change is expensive, said in one checkable sentence.

choices.text: We should use the strategy pattern here
choices.why: That is an answer looking for a question, the habit the section opens with.

choices.text: Every good codebase uses at least three patterns
choices.why: A count of patterns says nothing about any pressure on this code.

prompt: The fine function's if/elif has been edited twice in three years, and no change is planned. What does the section recommend?

choices.text: A strategy class per category, so the next change is cheap
choices.why: There is no next change in sight; that is building for a force that has not arrived.

choices.text: Leave it
choices.why: Right. No force, so the right change is none: three branches anybody reads in ten seconds.

choices.text: A dictionary of rates, since a table reads better than an if statement
choices.why: The table is the answer when categories keep arriving; here none are arriving.

prompt: Two pieces of code are identical. In one repository the function changes every month; in the other it has not changed in four years. What follows?

choices.text: Each deserves its own design
choices.why: Right. The force lives in the history and the plan, not in the text of the code.

choices.text: They need the same design, because the code is the same
choices.why: The section showed one function with three right answers, decided by facts outside it.

choices.text: The stable one should get the pattern first, because it is safer to change
choices.why: Safety to change is not a reason to change; the stable one has no force pushing on it.

prompt: In the hops.py run, how many function calls did layered.py make to write one notice?
Where does the section say most of a pattern's cost falls?

choices.text: On the machine, which runs the extra calls
choices.why: Nine calls instead of one cost microseconds; the section does not measure speed.

choices.text: On the author, once, when the classes are first written
choices.why: That is the small part, according to the section.

choices.text: On every reader, every time
choices.why: Right. The hops recur on every reading for as long as the code lives.

prompt: A rule changes every week in code that is read about once a month. By the section's measure, how much indirection has it earned?

choices.text: Little: indirection pays in code that seldom changes
choices.why: That is backwards; indirection pays by absorbing change.

choices.text: A lot: frequent change, rare reading
choices.why: Right. The change costs more than the readers' extra hops, so the pattern earns its place.

choices.text: Exactly one layer, whatever the rates are
choices.why: The section gives a comparison of two rates, not a fixed allowance.

choices.text: It cannot be judged until the code has a second implementation
choices.why: The rates of change and of reading are known here, and they are what the measure uses.

prompt: Fowler's name for hooks and abstractions built for a future nobody can point to is speculative ___ .
smells.py reports a protocol with one implementation. When is that structure still right?

choices.text: It is not; a protocol with one implementation is a class with a second name
choices.why: The section says to read each line as a question, and names the case below.

choices.text: When the protocol has more than one method
choices.why: The number of methods does not change whether anything else can stand in that place.

choices.text: When the tests hold a fake as the second one
choices.why: Right. The program never opened the test file, which is why it reports a question and not a verdict.

prompt: Which of these is a sign of UNDER-design rather than over-design?

choices.text: The same if over categories appears in five places
choices.why: Right. A force has arrived, and every new category means finding all five.

choices.text: A parameter that every caller passes and no method reads
choices.why: That is speculative generality: structure for a change that has not come.

choices.text: A factory that only ever builds one class
choices.why: That is over-design, one of the four signs in the section.

choices.text: A service method that only hands the call on to another object
choices.why: A forwarding layer is listed among the signs of over-design.

prompt: In case 1, why is the member category put in a dictionary of rates and not in a strategy class per category?

choices.text: Dictionaries are faster to look up than classes
choices.why: Speed is not part of the argument in any of the three cases.

choices.text: The category changes a number, and a number is data
choices.why: Right. A new category is one line of data and no new code.

choices.text: Python cannot store classes as values in a dictionary
choices.why: It can; RULES stores functions, and classes are objects too.

prompt: In case 2, what would turn the in-process list of listeners into a queue between processes?

choices.text: A fourth listener, the reservations desk, being added next year
choices.why: One more listener is one more entry in the list; the observer already absorbs that.

choices.text: The e-mail moving to another service, or no return being allowed to be lost in a crash
choices.why: Right. Those are the forces a broker answers, and the section names them as the reopening condition.

choices.text: The listeners taking more than a second to run
choices.why: Slowness is lesson 18's question about threads, not a reason given for a broker.

prompt: Case 3 needed to prove when a book was returned. Why was full event sourcing rejected?

choices.text: Event sourcing cannot record the time an event happened
choices.why: It records exactly that; the problem is everything else it brings.

choices.text: Two columns, returned_by and returned_at, answer every dispute
choices.why: They lose the earlier value when a return is corrected, which the section points out.

choices.text: Nothing asked to rebuild state from history
choices.why: Right. An append-only table answers the audit without making the log the source of truth.

prompt: Match each shape found in code to the pattern it usually is.

pairs.left: Holds an object of its own interface and forwards to it, adding something
Holds an object of another interface and offers yours
A dictionary from names to constructors
Holds one of a family and delegates one step to it

prompt: In mystery.py, what makes PartnerCatalogue an adapter rather than a decorator?

choices.text: What it holds is not a Catalogue
choices.why: Right. It offers Catalogue over nested dictionaries in another library's format.

choices.text: It is created through the SOURCES dictionary
choices.why: ShelfCatalogue is created the same way and is no adapter; how it is built is the factory's shape.

choices.text: Its name contains Partner, which marks an external system
choices.why: The section says to read structure first; a name proves nothing either way.

choices.text: It counts nothing, while CountingCatalogue counts every lookup made
choices.why: Counting is what this decorator adds; a decorator could add anything. The difference is what is held.

prompt: A class holds an object of its own interface and forwards to it, adding a cache. Is it a proxy or a decorator?

choices.text: A decorator, because a proxy cannot hold an object of its own interface
choices.why: A proxy holds exactly that; the two have the same structure.

choices.text: The structure cannot settle it; the two differ only in intent
choices.why: Right. Caching leans towards proxy, but only the commit message or the author can say what was meant.

choices.text: A proxy, because only proxies are allowed to cache
choices.why: No rule restricts caching to one pattern; the table says caching usually signals a proxy.

prompt: What happens to an ADR when its decision changes?

choices.text: It is edited to describe the new decision
choices.why: Editing it erases the history of why the code took each shape.

choices.text: It is deleted, since it no longer applies
choices.why: A deleted record takes the old argument with it, which is what records exist to keep.

choices.text: A new one is written, and the old one is marked superseded
choices.why: Right. The history then reads in order, which a commit log tells badly.

prompt: Which part of a pattern decision record does the section say is most often left out?

choices.text: The date
choices.why: Every record in the format carries a status line with a date.

choices.text: The condition that would reopen the decision
choices.why: Right. Without it the reader has to guess whether the choice still applies.

choices.text: A description of the code that implements the decision
choices.why: The section says the record should not describe the code, which the code already does.

prompt: A reviewer finds a protocol with one implementation and proposes removing it. An ADR beside it says a second implementation is planned for June. What did the ADR save?

choices.text: Undoing a deliberate choice, and making it again in June
choices.why: Right. Without the record the "fix" loses the argument and someone rebuilds the protocol later.

choices.text: Little, since a protocol with one implementation is over-design whatever is planned
choices.why: A planned second implementation is a stated force with a date; that is the case the record exists for.

choices.text: The test that would otherwise fail
choices.why: Removing an unused protocol breaks no test; what is lost is the reason for it.

prompt: Put the first four checklist questions in the order the section asks them.
items: What is the force, in one sentence?
What does it cost a reader?
trap: Starting from the answer, or from its cost, skips the question that can stop the whole thing early.

prompt: Before collapsing a layer that seems to only forward calls, what does the section say to look for?

choices.text: Whether the layer's file is longer than fifty lines
choices.why: Length is not one of the questions; what the layer does is.

choices.text: A rule or a translation the layer performs
choices.why: Right. Removing a pattern deserves the same evidence as adding one.

choices.text: Whether a design patterns book names the layer
choices.why: A name in a book is not a force in this code.

choices.text: Whether the original author still works on the team and can approve the change
choices.why: The evidence is in the code and its records, which is why the section asks for both.

prompt: Which checklist question comes from lesson 18?

choices.text: What would reopen the decision?
choices.why: That comes from the worked decisions and the ADR section of this lesson.

choices.text: What is the smallest answer?
choices.why: That leans on lesson 6's point about patterns built into the language.

choices.text: Who else might be here at the same time?
choices.why: Right. A lazy singleton or a changing observer list is a new bug under threads.

prompt: A pull request adds NotifierFactory, Notifier (a protocol), EmailNotifier and NotifierConfig, for the one way the library sends notices. Which questions should the review ask? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Which force do these answer, in one sentence?
choices.why: Right. The first checklist question, and the one that can end the review early.

choices.text: Is there a second Notifier, even a fake in the tests?
choices.why: Right. A protocol with one implementation and no double is the first sign of over-design.

choices.text: Does each class follow the naming convention of the pattern it implements?
choices.why: Names are the poorest guide to a pattern; tidy names on unneeded classes are still unneeded.

choices.text: Can the factory build anything other than EmailNotifier?
choices.why: Right. A factory that can only make one thing is one of the four signs.

prompt: The library adds a fourth and a fifth way to fine items, each with its own configuration that staff edit. Case 1 chose a dictionary of functions. What now?

choices.text: Keep the functions; the decision was recorded and records are final
choices.why: A record is never edited, but it is superseded when its reopening condition arrives.

choices.text: The reopening condition has arrived: a small class per rule, recorded in a new ADR
choices.why: Right. Rules with their own configuration were exactly what the record said would change the choice.

choices.text: Move to event sourcing, since the rules now change over time
choices.why: Nothing asks to rebuild state from history; this is the strategy question, not the audit one.

prompt: A colleague says layered.py is better design than plain.py because it follows more principles from this course. What is the strongest answer?

choices.text: Principles do not matter in Python
choices.why: The course applies them in Python throughout; the point is when they pay.

choices.text: plain.py is faster, and speed is what matters most
choices.why: The lesson never argued from speed; nine calls cost microseconds.

choices.text: Ask which force each layer answers here
choices.why: Right. Each class is a sound pattern answering a force this program does not have.

choices.text: layered.py has more lines, so it is harder to test
choices.why: Line count is not testability; the layers would make a fake policy easy, if anybody needed one.
